A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, despite substantial retitling and refocusing. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison; retained equations, code and attention visualizations establish continuity.

before.justification: v1 reports original head-zeroing experiments on five benchmarks, pretraining-checkpoint measurements, input-text analyses and appendix ablations.

after.justification: v2 reports original MMLU interventions comparing 13 scoring functions across 14 models, plus score-overlap and distribution analyses.

M1.justification: v2 expands identification into 13 scoring functions covering attention entropy, value-vector norms, head-output norms and normalization variants. HONOR is retained unchanged as Avg Head Output Norm (LN), and First Token becomes Avg Weight of First Token (AWFT). The additional scoring procedures substantially expand the method beyond these renamed components.

E1.justification: MMLU and FineWeb-Edu remain, but ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, WinoGrande and GSM8K evaluations disappear, including from the appendices. This substantially narrows evaluated task coverage and removes the open-ended mathematical-generation test.

E2.justification: The intervention comparisons expand from HONOR, First Token and random selection to 13 scoring functions plus random selection, verified in v2 Figures 3 and 6. Added comparators include entropy-based, value-norm and last-token-output rules and their normalized variants. The two principal earlier methods remain under new names.

E3.justification: MMLU changes from 0-shot to 5-shot, and intervention models expand from six base models to 14 base/finetuned configurations. Fixed threshold ranges are replaced by seven score-quantile thresholds targeting 0–30% head removal, with normalized AUC added for ranking. The overlap analysis changes from four benchmark datasets at approximately 14% selection to 100 FineWeb-Edu sequences at approximately 10%.

E4.justification: v1's pretraining trajectories, text-characteristic regressions, layerwise dormancy, intervention-propagation, Gaussian-replacement and first-token-depth analyses are removed. v2 expands scoring-rule overlap analysis and adds score-distribution comparisons across model sizes, finetuning stages and input datasets. The attention-sink and PCA examples are retained rather than newly added.

E5.justification: v1 Section 4.4 reports regression correlations as statistically significant at p < 0.01; this significance reporting disappears with that analysis. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or performance error bars.

E6.justification: The benchmark results are substantially replaced. v1 Table 1 reports HONOR removing 14.9–25.6% of heads within a one-percentage-point accuracy tolerance averaged over four tasks. v2 Table 2 reports averages of 12.18% for the best non-AWFT scorer versus 4.61% for AWFT on 5-shot MMLU. These are different settings, not a direct performance change. New overlap, ranking and finetuning/scale findings replace many earlier results.

T1.justification: v2 Table 1 and Section 3 substantially expand the mathematical definitions from the two principal threshold rules to a taxonomy spanning six base scores and their normalization variants. The original HONOR equation is retained. The change concerns formal definitions; neither version presents original theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contribution changes from one dormant-head definition plus emergence and input-characteristic findings to a taxonomy, comparative scoring evaluation and scale/finetuning findings. The abstract and conclusion replace multi-benchmark and open-ended claims with MMLU-specific inactivity estimates and a quantified claim that AWFT undercounts inactive heads.

C2.justification: v2 removes interpretations concerning dormant-to-active transitions challenging mutual reinforcement, text density, and the first token's depth-dependent role. It adds interpretations of finetuning preserving attention behavior and larger models developing different specialization, qualifying the scale attribution because Qwen training-token budgets are unknown. Appendix A.4 also proposes sequence length as an explanation for dataset-dependent AWFT distributions.

D1.justification: The two PyTorch implementations remain under renamed descriptions. v2 adds automatic-batching guidance and an explicit OLMo-2 float16 exception, while removing alphabet-density code and some exact input/display-processing details for retained visualizations. FineWeb truncation is inconsistently documented as starting at 10 tokens in Section 4.1 or 30 tokens in Appendix A.4.

R1.justification: The core attention-sink and head-pruning literature remains. v2 adds Rafailov et al. (2023), Lambert et al. (2024) and Sun et al. (2025), removes several dataset and mechanism references, and describes its interventions as dynamic pruning. The earlier explicit challenge to Guo et al.'s mutual-reinforcement explanation disappears.

P1.justification: The title and terminology change from dormant heads and HONOR to inactive heads and descriptive scoring-function names. The abstract, introduction, method exposition, experimental narrative and conclusion are extensively rewritten, while the related-work order and appendix organization are substantially revised.

P2.justification: A taxonomy schematic, score-definition table, overlap/ranking heatmaps and distribution panels replace most earlier displays. Intervention figures and summary tables are redesigned for the expanded scorer/model comparisons. v1 Figures 2 and 6 are retained as v2 Figures 10 and 11, but relocated and resized.

improvement.justification: The taxonomy, quantile-based threshold selection and expanded model comparisons strengthen the investigation of scoring rules. However, MMLU-only validation removes four benchmarks, including generation, and several informative robustness analyses. Reporting also remains problematic: v2 Table 2 claims deficits versus AWFT below 0.3 percentage points, but its Qwen2.5-14B row reports a 1.17-point deficit. The substantial gains in comparative analysis and losses in validation breadth prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
